name: DeepLIFT
description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains neural network predictions by decomposing the difference between the actual output and a reference output back to individual input features. It compares each neuron's activation to a reference activation (typically from a baseline input like all zeros or the dataset mean) and propagates these differences backwards through the network using chain rule modifications. Unlike gradient-based methods, DeepLIFT satisfies the sensitivity property (zero input gets zero attribution) and provides more stable attributions by using discrete differences rather than gradients.

name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains neural network predictions by working backwards through the network to show how much each input feature contributed to the final decision. It follows a simple conservation rule: the total contribution scores always add up to the original prediction. Starting from the output, LRP distributes 'relevance' backwards through each layer using different rules depending on the layer type. This creates a detailed breakdown showing which input features helped or hindered the prediction, making it easier to understand why the network made a particular decision.

The coefficients of this local surrogate model reveal which features most influenced the specific prediction.

name: Factor Analysis
description: Factor analysis is a statistical technique that identifies latent variables (hidden factors) underlying observed correlations in data. It works by analysing how variables relate to each other, finding a smaller number of unobserved factors that explain patterns among multiple observed variables. Unlike PCA which maximises total variance, factor analysis focuses on shared variance (communalities - the variance variables have in common) whilst separating out unique variance and measurement error. After extracting factors, rotation methods like varimax (which creates uncorrelated factors) or oblimin (allowing correlated factors) help make factors more interpretable by aligning them with distinct groups of variables.

It identifies 'pertinent negatives' (minimal features that could be removed to change the prediction) and 'pertinent positives' (minimal features that must be present to maintain the prediction). This approach helps users understand not just what led to a decision, but what would need to change to achieve a different outcome, providing actionable insights for decision-making.

name: RuleFit
description: RuleFit creates interpretable surrogate models that can explain complex black-box models or serve as interpretable alternatives. It works by learning a sparse linear model that combines automatically extracted decision rules with original features. The technique first builds tree ensembles to generate candidate rules, then uses LASSO regression to select the most important rules and features. The resulting model provides global explanations through human-readable rules (e.g., 'IF age > 50 AND income < 30k THEN ...') combined with linear feature weights, making complex model behaviour transparent and auditable.

name: Differential Privacy
description: Differential privacy provides mathematically rigorous privacy protection by adding carefully calibrated random noise to data queries, statistical computations, or machine learning outputs. The technique works by ensuring that the presence or absence of any individual's data has minimal impact on the results - specifically, any query result should be nearly indistinguishable whether or not a particular person's data is included. This is achieved through controlled noise addition that scales with the query's sensitivity and a privacy budget (epsilon) that quantifies the privacy-utility trade-off. The smaller the epsilon, the more noise is added and the stronger the privacy guarantee, but at the cost of reduced accuracy.

name: Quantile Regression
description: Quantile regression estimates specific percentiles (quantiles) of the target variable rather than just predicting the average outcome. For example, instead of predicting 'average house price = £300,000', it can predict 'there's a 10% chance the price will be below £250,000, 50% chance below £300,000, and 90% chance below £380,000'. This technique reveals how input features affect different parts of the outcome distribution - perhaps property size strongly influences luxury homes (90th percentile) but barely affects budget properties (10th percentile). By capturing the full conditional distribution, quantile regression provides rich uncertainty information and enables robust prediction intervals.

name: Conformal Prediction
description: Conformal prediction provides mathematically guaranteed uncertainty quantification by creating prediction sets that contain the true outcome with a specified probability (e.g., exactly 95% coverage). The technique works by measuring how 'strange' or 'nonconforming' new predictions are compared to calibration data - if a prediction seems unusual, it gets wider intervals. For example, in medical diagnosis, instead of saying 'likely cancer', it might say 'possible diagnoses: {cancer, benign tumour} with 95% confidence'. This distribution-free method works with any underlying model (neural networks, random forests, etc.) and requires no assumptions about data distribution, making it a robust framework for reliable uncertainty estimates in high-stakes applications.

name: Platt Scaling
description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. name: Temperature Scaling
description: Temperature scaling adjusts a model's confidence by applying a single parameter (temperature) to its predictions. When a model is too confident in its wrong answers, temperature scaling can fix this by making the predictions more realistic. It works by dividing the model's outputs by the temperature value before converting them to probabilities. Higher temperatures make the model less confident, whilst lower temperatures increase confidence. name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) measures model performance by plotting precision (the proportion of positive predictions that are correct) against recall (the proportion of actual positives that are correctly identified) at various classification thresholds, then calculating the area under the resulting curve. Unlike accuracy or AUC-ROC, AUPRC is particularly valuable for imbalanced datasets where the minority class is of primary interest---a perfect score is 1.0, whilst random performance equals the positive class proportion. name: Algorithm Review Boards
description: An algorithm review board is a standing, multidisciplinary body inside an organisation that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects at set points and decides whether, and on what conditions, they may proceed. The literature also calls these bodies AI ethics boards or AI review boards. They differ from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because they also weigh harms to the people a system will affect and to society. A risk-based triage decides which projects need full review; the project team then submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, and members drawn from technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds, sometimes with people from affected communities, question the team and iterate on that account with them. The board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects, and the output is a dated decision record with its reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built.

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers watch a deployed AI system's operational and model-level signals and automatically stop, limit or reroute calls to the model when those signals cross preset limits. The circuit breaker, a software resilience pattern, wraps calls to the model: while closed it passes requests through and counts failures in a rolling time window; when failures pass a threshold it opens, so further requests fail at once or receive a fallback such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person; after a cooldown it half-opens and lets a few trial requests through, closing again only if they succeed. For a machine learning model, what counts as a failure is widened from errors and timeouts to model-level signals available at the moment of prediction, such as input drift scores, low prediction confidence, out-of-range outputs or limits on the actions the system may take, because true accuracy usually cannot be measured until outcomes arrive later. The output is a log of breaker state changes, the metrics that triggered them and the alerts raised, which shows when and why the system was restricted; the protection is only as good as the chosen thresholds and the fallback behind the breaker.

name: Reweighing
description: Reweighing is a pre-processing method, from Kamiran and Calders (2012), that removes the statistical association between a protected attribute and the outcome label in training data by giving each training example a weight, without changing any feature values or labels. For every combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired), the weight is the number of examples that combination would have if group and label were independent, divided by the number it actually has: the group's share of the data times the label's share, over the combination's observed share. Combinations rarer than independence predicts, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so that in the weighted data every group has the same rate of positive labels. A model is then trained on the original data using these weights; the outputs are the weighted training set and a small table of weights that records exactly how each group-label combination was adjusted.

name: Trigger-Set Model Watermarking
description: Trigger-set model watermarking lets the owner of a trained classifier show later that a suspect model was copied from theirs, by planting a secret behaviour that only the owner can demonstrate. Before release, the owner chooses a small secret trigger set (in the originating scheme, 100 abstract images), gives each input a label the model would not otherwise predict, and trains or fine-tunes the model to return those labels while keeping its accuracy on the real task. In the originating scheme the owner also records cryptographic commitments to the trigger inputs and their labels, which fix the watermark at release so that a trigger set cannot be invented once a dispute has begun. To verify, the owner, or an arbiter shown the opened commitments, sends the trigger inputs to the suspect model through its ordinary prediction interface and counts how many return the assigned labels; an independently trained model matches them at about chance level, so a match rate above a preset threshold is evidence of copying. The technique produces the watermarked model, the commitments and, for each verification, the suspect model's trigger-set accuracy against the threshold.

name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score.
